parts.note: correct as in proper, fitting the rules of etiquette
ties are worn round the neck

explanation.surface: A dress-code note on what makes neckwear acceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: Properties are the qualities or attributes that belong to something, its characteristics.

definitions.meaning: to proceed is to go forward, so 'goes' is the verb form
the money brought in from a sale or event

explanation.surface: Someone walks off with the day's cash.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the verb, advances onward; the other is the noun for revenue raised, as in the proceeds of a raffle.

clue.text: One has to reverse at a green light in New Zealand

parts.note: O stands for one, the figure looking like the numeral 0

indicators.note: to reverse tells us to turn the word at round so it reads backwards

parts.note: a green light is the signal to go

explanation.surface: A driver backing up at a traffic signal somewhere in New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One has' reads as a person doing the reversing, but 'has' is a link; 'to reverse' turns only the little word 'at', and the green light is the signal to go.
explanation.definitionFit: Otago is a region of New Zealand's South Island, so it is a place found in that country.

parts.note: alludes to the old saying, attributed to Froissart, that a certain nation takes its pleasures sadly

explanation.surface: A gloomy party of holidaymakers.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'they take their pleasures sadly' was said of the people of England, so glum pleasure-seekers are those people.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverbial description of a national character: people who seek enjoyment yet look miserable doing so.

indicators.note: curious here means odd or strange, signalling that the letters are put into a strange new order

parts.note: the Tate Gallery stands on the bank of the Thames in London, so the gallery's is TATE'S

explanation.surface: A remark on the peculiar judgement shown by a London riverside art gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is the London art gallery on the Thames; 'curious' rearranges TATES.
explanation.definitionFit: Taste is the ability to judge what is fine or fitting, a synonym of discernment.

indicators.note: of signals that the letters are taken out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone is driven from the county of Essex in a disorderly rush.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'EssEX PELl-mell'. Essex is an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: To expel is to drive or force someone out, as from a school or a country.

clue.text: It's not the young who are spoiled by the pill

indicators.note: by places the pill beside the word sought, and taking that pill away from the plundered word leaves the remainder

parts.note: spoiled in the old sense of plundered, stripped of goods by force
the pill is taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark that the people ruined by the contraceptive pill are not the young.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests medicine, but 'spoiled' means plundered: PILL placed by the answer makes PILLAGED, so removing PILL leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who are not young are the elderly, people advanced in years.

parts.note: reads as someone storming out and banging the door of a bridge room, while also naming the bridge contract that wins all thirteen tricks

explanation.surface: A bridge player storms out of the card room.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'slam' is the bang of a door shut in anger, and in bridge a slam is winning every trick, the biggest being the grand one.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge the top contract takes all thirteen tricks; a slammed door is the angry exit.

clue.text: What the doctor ordered, ditto pundit

parts.note: DO is the abbreviation for ditto, meaning the same again
a pundit is a learned person, a sage

explanation.surface: A patient repeats the doctor's instructions word for word, like an expert.
explanation.definitionFit: A dosage is the amount of medicine a physician prescribes to be taken.

parts.note: a peck is a dry measure, but also what a bird does when eating small bits of bread

explanation.surface: Bread sold by the peck, an old dry measure.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a quantity of bread measured in pecks; the cryptic reading is what birds peck up, the tiny scraps.
explanation.definitionFit: Small fragments of bread, the sort scattered for birds to peck at.

clue.text: The sweeter of two things the bells said

definitions.text: The sweeter of two things the bells said

parts.words: The sweeter of two things the bells said
parts.note: recalls the nursery rhyme in which the bells of St Clement's name two kinds of citrus fruit

explanation.surface: A riddle about the two words church bells chime.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme runs 'Oranges and lemons, say the bells of St Clement's'; of those two fruits the lemons are sour, so the sweeter is the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme pairs two citrus fruits, and the less sharp of them is the sweet one of the pair.

clue.text: Maybe it was grand for Bishop Blougram

definitions.meaning: maybe means possibly

definitions.text: it was grand for Bishop Blougram
definitions.meaning: in Browning's poem 'Bishop Blougram's Apology' the bishop speaks of 'the grand ...'

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a fictional bishop had a splendid time.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Browning's dramatic monologue has the bishop refer to the uncertainty of faith as 'the grand Perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses use the word meaning possibly: once plainly, once as Browning's phrase for the great uncertainty.

clue.text: Note reason for crime: it's exciting

parts.note: E is one of the musical notes
a motive is the reason that leads someone to commit a crime

explanation.surface: A detective's jotting about why a crime happened, finding the case thrilling.
explanation.definitionFit: Emotive means stirring feelings, arousing strong emotion.

parts.note: plays on the saying about helping a crippled animal over a stile: the made-up word stilish means stile-like, and this jumper cannot clear one

explanation.surface: A remark that some jumper is not stylish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stilish' sounds like stylish, and the jumper seems a sweater; it is really a dog unable to jump a stile, as in 'help a lame dog over a stile'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hound that is crippled in a leg cannot leap a farm fence, so it is no jumper of stiles.

parts.note: dun is a dull greyish-brown colour
can means is able, so it expresses capability

explanation.surface: Capability Brown, the English landscape gardener, put forward in place of a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Capability Brown was an 18th-century English landscape gardener; here the two words are split. Duncan is the Scottish king in Macbeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Duncan was a king of Scotland, the monarch murdered in Shakespeare's Macbeth.

clue.text: It makes a clean job of fingertip control

definitions.text: It makes a clean job of fingertip control

parts.words: It makes a clean job of fingertip control
parts.note: reads like praise for precise handiwork, but describes the tool that scrubs dirt from under the tips of the fingers

explanation.surface: Something that handles a delicate manual task neatly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fingertip control' suggests dexterity; the real sense is keeping the fingertips, the nails, clean.
explanation.definitionFit: A small stiff brush used to scrub the hands and clean under the fingertips.

parts.note: a fortress that cannot be taken is a ..., and in Goldsmith's play the squire of that name is mistaken for an innkeeper

explanation.surface: A landlord in a Goldsmith work who cannot be overcome.
explanation.walkthrough: In Oliver Goldsmith's comedy 'She Stoops to Conquer', young Marlow mistakes Mr Hardcastle's house for an inn and treats him as the landlord, hence the quotation marks.
explanation.definitionFit: The squire in Goldsmith's comedy, taken for an innkeeper; his name splits into words for a fort that cannot be stormed.

definitions.meaning: One of the Small Isles of the Inner Hebrides, Scotland
the spirit issued as a daily ration to sailors, which disappears down their throats

explanation.surface: An island is ceded and the Navy has lost it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a naval defeat; the drink that the Navy swallows (the sailors' daily ration) is what is 'lost to' it.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a Hebridean isle; the other is the sailors' traditional drink, which vanishes when drunk.

definitions.meaning: the proverb says one swallow does not make a summer, so more than one might
the birds of that name are swift, fast fliers

explanation.surface: Musing on a proverb about summer and things that fly quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One swallow does not make a summer', so the plural is what a proverbial summer would need.
explanation.definitionFit: Several of those migrant birds make up the summer of the saying, and they are noted for quick flight.

clue.text: August follower is one over the eight

definitions.meaning: the month that comes after August is September
the eight here is the eighth month, and one more than that is the next; the phrase is also slang for being drunk

explanation.surface: A man who follows the calendar has had one drink too many.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One over the eight' is British slang for slightly drunk, after eight pints; here it means the month after the eighth.
explanation.definitionFit: September follows August and stands one place after August, the eighth in the calendar.

definitions.note: the definition is a noun phrase but the answer is the adjective describing such a display

parts.note: too means to an excessive degree
thy is the old form of your

explanation.surface: Someone says your grin shows rather too many teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: Ivories is slang for teeth; a toothy grin is one that shows a lot of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivories are teeth, and an adjective for a grin that bares many of them describes such a display.

clue.text: Rattiness finally led to depopulation here

definitions.text: Rattiness finally led to depopulation here

parts.words: Rattiness finally led to depopulation here
parts.note: rattiness is both irritability and being overrun by rodents; in the legend the plague of rodents led to the piper taking the town's children away

explanation.surface: Bad temper at last drove people out of some town.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Pied Piper legend the German town is plagued by rats; when it refuses to pay the piper who cleared them, he leads its children away.
explanation.definitionFit: The German town of the Pied Piper legend, overrun by rats and then emptied of its children.

definitions.meaning: to cut grass or hay
14 across begins DUN, and placed with it this word makes Dunmow, the Essex town famous for the Dunmow Flitch, a side of bacon

explanation.surface: Someone asks about a cut of bacon from a king.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dunmow Flitch is a side of bacon awarded at Great Dunmow in Essex to married couples who have not quarrelled for a year; 'at 14' puts the word after DUN.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut grass is to mow it, and it completes the name of the bacon town when joined to DUN.

definitions.meaning: to spare something is to manage without it, as in 'can you spare it?'
spare parts kept in reserve to replace broken ones

explanation.surface: A mechanic manages without any additional components.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the verb, manages without; the other is the noun for replacement parts kept in reserve.

indicators.note: served as food is dished up, here the letters are dished up in a new order

explanation.surface: A rib chop served steaming at table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piping hot' suggests the chop; the definition means stirring bagpipe music. 'served' rearranges RIBCHOP.
explanation.definitionFit: A pibroch is a set of martial variations for the Highland bagpipe, so a fiery tune for pipers.

parts.note: seems to name a monarch before Queen Victoria, but a victoria is a light carriage, and what goes before it is the animal pulling it

explanation.surface: A question about the king before Queen Victoria.
explanation.walkthrough: Victoria's predecessor was William IV, the obvious false path; a victoria is a four-wheeled carriage, and the animal in the shafts goes in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The draught animal is harnessed in front of the light open carriage named after the queen.

parts.note: plaything means a thing played, the instrument Miriam and the maidens play in Exodus and the Psalms

explanation.surface: A toy belonging to a young woman in the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plaything' looks like a toy but is the instrument she plays; Miriam leads the women with a hand drum in Exodus 15.
explanation.definitionFit: A timbrel is a tambourine-like hand drum, which the women of the Bible played in celebration.

definitions.meaning: an extra shout added after three cheers is called a ...
the big striped wild feline

explanation.surface: A remarkably cheerful cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Three cheers and a tiger' is an old form, the extra cry after the cheers being the tiger.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the big striped feline and the extra yell added after three cheers.

parts.note: in Robert Southey's ballad 'The Inchcape Rock'

explanation.surface: Asks for the wrecker in a Southey poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Southey's ballad tells how a rover cut away the warning bell on the Inchcape Rock off Scotland and was later wrecked there himself.
explanation.definitionFit: The rover in Southey's ballad removes the reef's warning bell, sabotaging it, and is first-named so.

definitions.note: the definition includes is, the answer being the comparative adjective

indicators.note: we hear tells us the word for a trumper is to be taken by its sound

parts.note: in card games to ruff is to trump, so one who trumps is a ruffer

explanation.surface: Someone who trumps at cards is said to be more ill-mannered.
explanation.walkthrough: The feed reads 'Trumpet'; the page prints 'Trumper', one who trumps, a ruffer, which sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Rougher is the comparative of rough, meaning more coarse or ill-mannered, so ruder.

parts.note: an earth-mover suggests a digger, but here is the astronomer who, after recanting, is said to have muttered under his breath that the earth still moves

explanation.surface: A quietly spoken operator of digging machinery.
explanation.walkthrough: The astronomer, forced to deny that the earth goes round the sun, is said to have whispered 'Eppur si muove' (and yet it moves).
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian astronomer set the earth in motion round the sun and supposedly said so under his breath.

clue.text: Call for hare down Greek Street way ?

definitions.meaning: ... was the huntsman's cry on sighting a hare
Greek Street is a street in the London district of that name

explanation.surface: A huntsman calling after a hare along a London street.
explanation.walkthrough: Soho is a district of central London containing Greek Street; its name comes from the old hunting cry.
explanation.definitionFit: The old hunting cry on spotting a hare also names the London district that contains Greek Street.

clue.text: Goes back to wartime digs to economize?

definitions.meaning: returns to the trenches, the dug-outs of the First World War
the answer is the third-person form, cuts down on spending

explanation.surface: A veteran revisits wartime lodgings to save money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digs' looks like lodgings but means trenches; going back to them is to re-trench.
explanation.definitionFit: Cutting expenses is to retrench, and read in two parts it is to return to the trenches.
